metadata.title: Nvidia’s Board Had Other Options: Robert Maciejko

content.text:
By Robert Maciejko
Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia Corp. (Nasdaq: NVDA). The stock jumped more than 30% on the news, after losing about a third of its value in two weeks. I understand why. What interests me more than the last decision is what the board could have done in the eleven days before it.
The public record is short. On Nov. 8 the board opened an independent inquiry. On Nov. 12 the company announced Huang's resignation, made its CFO interim CEO and named its first board chair. On Nov. 17 the chair said the board "does not intend to reinstate" him. On Nov. 23 Nvidia announced a unanimous vote to bring him back. The inquiry is still running.
I can defend either decision. A founder who built that much value deserves protection from a rush to judgment. He doesn't get protection from the rules or the law. Even the Nov. 17 "no" made sense to me. Huang had just said in public that he'd be honored to come back, and no serious candidate takes the job while the founder waits at the door.
The sequence is harder to defend. Out, then "no," then back, all before the board's own inquiry has reported. The board says it was satisfied with Huang's candor and that input from senior levels of the US government left it confident on national security. President Trump told CNBC the same day that the directors asked for that assurance, that his administration gave it, and that he "convinced" them. Nvidia hasn't said how independently it weighed that input, or whether it would have reached the same decision without it.
I published a short piece on this with three co-authors: Ludo Van der Heyden, founding director of INSEAD's Corporate Governance Centre; Theodoros Evgeniou, Professor of Technology and Business at INSEAD; and technology entrepreneur Yann Lechelle. They wrote INSEAD's analysis of the OpenAI board crisis in 2023. Our view is that this board had more options than it used, and it had them from the first day.
-
Take responsibility at board level. When a CEO goes wrong, the board has often been asleep. Name a visibly independent chair or lead director and commit to refreshing a board whose members have served about 15 years on average. Nvidia named its first chair only as its CEO left, and picked a director who has served since 1993.
-
Ask the CEO to step aside, not out. An acting CEO buys time for the facts. Much of what the board did after Huang left, including talking to the government, it could have done with him on leave.
-
Widen the inquiry. Have it cover the board's own oversight, and say so.
-
Consider another role. President next to a new CEO, or a board seat.
-
Consult the government and keep the decision. Listen carefully to the state on national security. Who runs the company is still for the directors to decide, and to be seen to decide.
-
Set terms for a return. A named successor, assurances on conduct, a date to review the arrangement.
